How Crop Improvement Works: Genes, Pollination and Hybrid Seed

Before you can judge a seed, you need to know how plants pass traits to their seed. This module explains pollination, Mendel's simple rules of inheritance, what makes a hybrid different from an open-pollinated variety, and how to turn your farm's main problem into a clear breeding or selection goal.
From Mendel to Your Field: Genes, Traits and Pollination
Explain the difference between a plant's genes and the conditions it grows in
Classify common Nigerian crops as mainly self-pollinated or cross-pollinated

Every crop improvement method, from a farmer picking her best cobs to a research institute releasing a new hybrid, rests on one idea: some of what you see in a plant is passed on through its **genes**, and some is caused by its **environment** (soil, rain, weeds, pests, fertiliser). Breeders write this as a simple rule: what you see (the **phenotype**) comes from the genes (the **genotype**) plus the environment. A tall, green maize plant on rich soil near a stream may have ordinary genes. A plant that stays green during a dry spell when its neighbours on the same soil wilt is more likely to carry useful genes.
A DNA double helix
Genes carried in DNA decide which traits a seed can pass on to the next crop.
Genes come in pairs

Most crop plants carry two copies of each gene, one from the mother plant (the one that bears the seed) and one from the father plant (the one that supplied the pollen). Different versions of the same gene are called **alleles**. When one allele hides the effect of the other, we call it **dominant**, and the hidden one **recessive**. In the 1860s the monk Gregor Mendel showed this with garden peas, and his rules still explain why seed saved from some crops stays the same while seed saved from others changes.
Worked example: a simple cross in maize grain colour
For example, Ngozi, a seed club member in Enugu State, crosses a pure yellow-grain maize with a pure white-grain maize. Yellow grain colour is dominant over white in maize.
Write the pure yellow parent as YY and the pure white parent as yy. Every pollen grain or egg carries one copy.
First generation (F1): every seed gets Y from one parent and y from the other, so all are Yy and all show yellow grain.
She plants the F1 seed and lets the plants pollinate each other. Each F1 plant passes on Y or y with equal chance.
Second generation (F2) combinations: YY, Yy, yY, yy. Three of the four contain at least one Y.
On an F2 cob with 400 kernels she expects about 3 out of 4 yellow: 400 x 3/4 = 300 yellow and 100 white.
The F1 looked uniform, but the next generation split into two types in roughly a 3 to 1 ratio. This splitting, called segregation, is the same reason saved hybrid seed does not stay true.
Pollination: who fathers the seed?

Seed forms only after pollen lands on the female part of a flower. In **self-pollinated** crops, the pollen usually comes from the same flower, so the plant is mostly its own father. Seed saved from a good self-pollinated variety stays very close to its parent year after year. In **cross-pollinated** crops, pollen travels from other plants, carried by wind or insects. Maize is the classic example: the tassel at the top sheds pollen, and the wind carries it to the silks of other plants, sometimes far across a field.

Traits farmers and breeders work on
**Yield potential:** grain, pods or fruit per plant and per hectare under good management.
**Maturity:** early varieties finish before the rains stop, useful in the drier north or for a second season.
**Resistance and tolerance:** for example to maize streak virus, the parasitic weed Striga, leaf diseases, or dry spells.
**Quality:** grain colour and texture buyers want, cooking time of beans, shelf life of tomato.
**Plant type:** height, lodging (falling over), how well the husk covers the cob against weevils and rain.
Simple traits and complex traits

Grain colour is controlled by one main gene, so it follows Mendel's ratio neatly. Yield and drought tolerance are controlled by many genes and are strongly affected by the environment. That is why a single good plant is weak evidence, and why later in this course you will compare varieties in replicated plots, not by looking at one cob.

Keep in mind that the environment also changes how genes show. A drought-tolerant variety planted in a waterlogged valley may look no better than local seed. This is why breeders test new lines in many locations and seasons before release, and why you should always compare seed on your own land under your normal conditions.
What you see in a plant is genes plus environment; only the genetic part is passed on in seed.
Dominant alleles hide recessive ones, so a uniform F1 can split into different types in the F2.
Self-pollinated crops keep their type in saved seed far more easily than cross-pollinated crops like maize.
Complex traits such as yield need careful comparison, not judgement from one plant.

Hybrids, Heterosis and Why Saved Hybrid Seed Disappoints
Define inbred line, hybrid vigour and F1 seed in plain words
Distinguish single-cross, three-way and double-cross hybrids
Compare a hybrid, an improved open-pollinated variety and a local variety
Calculate the seed cost difference of a hybrid versus a saved variety over several seasons

A **hybrid** variety is the first-generation offspring (the **F1**) of a deliberate cross between two different parents. In maize, breeders first create **inbred lines** by making plants pollinate themselves for several generations. Each inbred becomes very uniform but also weak and low-yielding, a loss of vigour called inbreeding depression. When two carefully chosen, unrelated inbreds are crossed, the F1 plants are often much stronger and higher-yielding than either parent. This boost is called **heterosis** or **hybrid vigour**.
An ear of maize
Maize is the crop where hybrid seed is most widely used, because its flowers make crossing easy.

Hybrids are common in maize, and in many vegetables such as tomato, cabbage, onion, cucumber and watermelon, where seed companies cross parent lines by hand or by using male-sterile plants. In rice, hybrid seed exists but is less common in Nigeria. For cowpea and soybean, almost all varieties farmers use are pure-line varieties, not hybrids.
Why saved hybrid seed lets you down

Remember Ngozi's yellow and white maize in the last lesson. The F1 was uniform because every plant had the same pair of parents. When you save seed from a hybrid field, the plants have pollinated each other, so the next crop is an F2. Its genes split into many combinations. You will see uneven plant heights, cobs of different sizes and maturity dates spread out, and the hybrid vigour drops sharply because many plants become more like the weak inbred parents. The exact loss depends on the hybrid and the season, so this course does not give one figure, but the drop is large enough that seed companies and extension services advise buying fresh hybrid seed every season.

Three kinds of seed in your village
**Local or farmer variety:** saved for years by families, well adapted to local taste and conditions, but often lower yielding and may carry seed-borne disease.

**Improved open-pollinated variety (OPV):** bred and released by a research institute, for example for streak virus resistance or early maturity. You can save its seed for a few seasons if you manage pollination and selection well.
**Hybrid:** bred for high yield and uniformity, usually from a seed company. You must buy it each season.
Worked example: seed cost over three seasons

For example, Halima farms 1 hectare of maize near Zaria. She is comparing a hybrid with an improved OPV. Seed prices here are illustrative only; check current prices with your agro-dealer. Both are sown at 20 kg per hectare.
Hybrid seed at about N5,000 per kg: 20 kg x N5,000 = N100,000 every season.
Three seasons of hybrid seed: N100,000 x 3 = N300,000.
Improved OPV certified seed at about N2,500 per kg in season 1: 20 kg x N2,500 = N50,000.
Seasons 2 and 3 she saves her own OPV seed. She keeps back 20 kg of grain each season, worth about N700 per kg as grain: 20 x N700 = N14,000 per season, or N28,000 for two seasons.
OPV total over three seasons: N50,000 + N28,000 = N78,000. Difference: N300,000 minus N78,000 = N222,000.

The hybrid costs about N222,000 more in seed over three seasons on 1 hectare. It is worth it only if its extra harvest, after extra fertiliser, is worth more than that. Module 3 shows how to test this with your own trial numbers.
Refresh saved OPV seed

Even a well-managed OPV slowly mixes with pollen from neighbouring fields and loses its purity. Many extension advisers suggest buying fresh certified seed of your OPV every few seasons. Ask your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) what they recommend for your crop.

Hybrid seed production also explains the price. To make single-cross maize seed, a seed company plants rows of the mother inbred and the father inbred in an isolated field, then removes the tassels from every mother plant by hand before they shed pollen, so the mother rows can only be fertilised by the father. Inbreds yield little, fields must be isolated and inspected, and all of this labour is paid for in the price of the bag.
A hybrid is the F1 of two chosen parents; its vigour comes from combining unrelated inbreds.
Single-cross hybrids are the most uniform; three-way and double-cross hybrids trade some uniformity for cheaper seed.
Seed saved from a hybrid becomes an F2 that segregates and loses much of its vigour.
Improved OPVs offer better genetics while still allowing seed saving for a few seasons.

Setting Your Improvement Goal and Readiness Check
Turn your farm's biggest crop problem into a specific improvement goal

Breeders never start with "a better maize". They start with a **product profile**: a short description of exactly what the new variety must do, for which farmers, in which environment. You can use the same discipline. A clear goal stops you being carried along by a colourful seed bag or a neighbour's single good harvest.
A woman working on a farm
A clear goal for your own field is the first step in choosing better seed.
From problem to goal
Name the problem in your own words, for example: "My maize dries before the cobs fill when the rains stop early."
Find the likely cause: is it the variety, the planting date, soil fertility, weeds or a pest? Check your past notes.
If the variety is part of the cause, name the trait you need: here, earlier maturity or drought tolerance.
Add the conditions: your zone, soil, rainfall pattern and the inputs you can actually afford.
Add the market: grain colour, size or taste your buyers pay for.
Not every problem is a seed problem

A new variety cannot fix late weeding, very poor soil or planting long after the rains are established. If your neighbours on similar land with the same seed harvest much more, look at management first. Changing seed and management at the same time makes it impossible to know which change helped.
Writing a variety profile

Split your traits into **must-have** (if a variety fails this, reject it) and **nice-to-have** (scored and weighed). For example, a must-have might be "matures in my season length" or "white grain, because my buyers are white maize millers". Nice-to-haves might be good husk cover, resistance to a leaf disease or short height for less lodging.
Worked example: ranking three candidate varieties

For example, Blessing farms in Niger State and wants earlier, more reliable maize. Two must-haves: white grain and maturity in her season. Three candidates pass. She gives each nice-to-have trait a weight (how much it matters to her) and a score from 1 to 5 using information from the ADP officer and seed dealers.
Weights: drought tolerance 4, yield potential 3, streak virus resistance 2, seed price 1 (total 10).
Variety A scores 4, 5, 3, 2. Weighted: 4x4 + 3x5 + 2x3 + 1x2 = 16 + 15 + 6 + 2 = 39.
Variety B scores 5, 3, 4, 4. Weighted: 20 + 9 + 8 + 4 = 41.
Variety C scores 2, 4, 2, 5. Weighted: 8 + 12 + 4 + 5 = 29.
She keeps the two highest scores, B and A, for her trial and drops C.
Variety B (41) and Variety A (39) go into the field trial alongside her usual seed. The scores only choose what to test; the trial on her own land makes the final decision.

Instead of asking an extension officer "Which seed is good?", ask: "Which white maize varieties that finish within my season have done well in trials in this local government area, and where can I buy certified seed of them?" Specific questions get useful answers.

Field Techniques: Controlled Crosses, Certified Seed and Replicated Trials

This module is hands-on. You will learn how breeders control pollination in maize and tomato, how farmers improve an open-pollinated variety by selection, how to check that bought seed is genuine and alive, how to handle treated and GM seed safely and legally, and how to run a replicated variety trial that gives trustworthy yield figures.
Controlled Pollination and Farmer Selection Techniques
Carry out a controlled hand pollination in maize using shoot and tassel bags
Emasculate and cross-pollinate a tomato flower
Run mass selection in an open-pollinated maize field without narrowing its genetic base
Use distance or planting time to isolate a seed plot

Breeding is controlled pollination. To make a cross you decide exactly which plant is the mother and which is the father, and you stop any other pollen from reaching the flower. To keep a variety pure you do the opposite: you keep outside pollen away. These skills let you make your own crosses for learning, produce clean seed of an OPV, and understand how seed companies make hybrid seed.
A person tending plants
Hand pollination is careful, patient work done in the early morning when pollen is fresh.
Hand pollination in maize

You need small paper or glassine **shoot bags** to cover the young ear, larger **tassel bags** made of strong paper, a stapler, a marker, a small knife or scissors and tags. Work on plants that are healthy and typical of their variety.
Cover the ear shoot with a shoot bag as soon as it appears from the leaf sheath, before any silk comes out. This stops stray pollen.

When silks have emerged under the bag (usually a few days later), cut the tip of the husk and silks straight across in the afternoon, so next morning the silks regrow as an even brush. Replace the shoot bag at once.
The same afternoon, cover the tassel of the chosen father plant with a tassel bag, folding it round the stem and stapling it. Shake gently first so old pollen falls off.
Next morning, after the dew dries and pollen starts shedding, bend the tassel, tap the bag so pollen falls inside, and remove it carefully.
Lift the shoot bag quickly, pour the pollen over the silk brush, and cover the ear straight away with the tassel bag, wrapping it round the stem and stapling it.
Write the cross on the bag and on a tag, mother first: for example "Local white x SAMMAZ variety, 12 Aug". Leave the bag on until harvest.
Maize hand pollination timing
Ear shoot appears: bag it
Silks emerge: cut back
Same afternoon: bag tassel
Next morning: collect pollen
Pollinate and cover ear
Label and leave to harvest
The whole cross takes about two days per ear, and timing matters more than equipment.
Crossing tomatoes

Tomato flowers usually pollinate themselves before they open, so you must remove the male parts first. This is called **emasculation**. Choose a bud on the mother plant that is swollen and yellowing but not yet open, usually the day before it would open.
With fine tweezers, gently open the petals and remove the cone of yellow anthers around the style. Do not damage the style.
Collect pollen from a fully open flower of the father plant by tapping or vibrating it over a fingernail or small dish.
Touch the pollen to the tip of the mother flower's style, the same day or the next morning.
Tie a thread or tag on the flower stalk with the cross name and date. If insects are active, cover the flower loosely with a small bag.
Harvest the fruit when fully ripe and save its seeds; they are F1 seeds of your cross.
Mass selection: improving an OPV in your own field

Most farmers do not need to make crosses. They can improve or maintain an open-pollinated variety by choosing seed parents carefully. The key mistake is choosing from too few plants, or choosing big cobs at the barn after harvest, when you no longer know how the plant grew. Select in the field, before harvest.
Worked example: a mass selection plan for OPV maize
For example, Funke grows 0.5 ha of an improved white OPV maize in Oyo State and wants to save her own seed for next season's 0.5 ha. Seed rate is 20 kg per hectare.
Seed needed: 0.5 ha x 20 kg = 10 kg. She plans to save 15 kg to allow for poor ears and a germination test.
She avoids the outer four rows on every side, where plants may be pollinated by a neighbour's maize and grow under different conditions.
Just before harvest she walks the inner field and ties a ribbon on plants that stand upright, are disease-free, have good husk cover and are not unusually isolated with extra space.
She marks at least 200 plants so the seed keeps a wide genetic base. Picking only a handful of plants would cause inbreeding and weaker seed.
She harvests the marked cobs separately, discards rotten or odd-coloured ones, and uses grain from the middle of each cob for seed.
Funke ends up with seed from many good plants across the field, enough for her next planting, with the genetic diversity that keeps an OPV vigorous.
Isolation by distance or by time

Maize pollen travels on the wind, so a seed plot needs space from other maize. Formal seed growers keep maize seed fields several hundred metres from other maize. If you cannot, plant your seed plot so it flowers several weeks earlier or later than nearby maize, and avoid saving seed from its border rows.
Controlling which pollen reaches the flower is the basis of every cross and every pure seed lot.
In maize, bag the ear before silks appear, bag the tassel, then pollinate and label.
Tomato crosses need emasculation of the bud before it opens.
Mass selection works best in the field, from many plants, away from the border rows.

The best genetics in the world cannot help if the seed in the bag is fake, old or dead. In Nigeria, the **National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC)** regulates the seed industry: it registers seed companies and certifies seed lots. Buying seed from a registered company or agro-dealer and checking the label protects your season.
A paper label tag
The seed label is your first evidence that the seed is what the seller says it is.
Seed classes
From breeder to farmer
Breeder seed
Foundation seed
Certified seed
Farmer's planting
Each class is multiplied from the one above it, under inspection, so that the variety stays true from the breeder to your field.

**Breeder seed** is produced in small amounts by the institute or company that bred the variety. It is multiplied into **foundation seed**, and foundation seed is multiplied into **certified seed**, which is what farmers buy. At each step, inspectors check that fields are isolated, that off-type plants are removed, and that seed lots meet purity and germination standards.
Reading the label
**Crop and variety name:** the exact variety, not just "improved maize".
**Seed class and lot number:** so the lot can be traced if there is a problem.
**Germination and purity results with a test date:** old test dates mean the seed may have aged.
**Producer name and address:** a company you can contact.
**Treatment:** if the seed is dressed with a fungicide or insecticide, the label should say so and name the chemical.
Signs of fake or poor seed

Be careful with seed sold loose from open sacks as "hybrid", bags with no lot number or test date, prices far below other dealers, bags that look re-stitched, or seed with many broken, shrivelled or mixed-colour grains. If in doubt, buy from a dealer your ADP or farmer group trusts, keep the receipt and the empty bag, and report suspected fake seed to NASC.
Test germination yourself

A simple test two weeks before planting tells you whether the seed is alive. Count out 100 seeds at random from the bag. Place them in rows of 10 on damp tissue, newspaper or a clean cloth, roll it loosely, keep it moist and warm, and count the seeds that have produced a healthy root and shoot after about 7 days for maize, or as the label suggests for other crops. For more confidence, do it as four sets of 25 or several sets of 100.
Worked example: adjusting seed rate after a germination test
For example, Ifeoma in Anambra tests a bag of OPV maize she saved last season. She plans 1 hectare at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm between plants, one plant per hole.
Target plant population: 10,000 m2 divided by (0.75 m x 0.25 m) = 10,000 / 0.1875 = about 53,333 plants per hectare.
Her test: 4 sets of 25 seeds sprouted 22, 21, 23 and 20. Total 86 out of 100, so germination is 86%.
Seeds needed if every seed grew: 53,333. Adjusted for 86%: 53,333 / 0.86 = about 62,015 seeds.
She weighs 100 seeds: 30 g, so 1 seed weighs about 0.3 g. Seed needed: 62,015 x 0.3 g = about 18,600 g, which is about 18.6 kg.
She adds a small margin for pests and buys or keeps 20 kg.

Instead of guessing, Ifeoma knows she needs about 18.6 kg plus a margin, and she knows the seed is alive. If germination is low, many advisers suggest buying fresh seed rather than simply sowing more.
Treated seed safety
Treated seed is poison, not food

Seed coated with a coloured powder or liquid has usually been dressed with a pesticide. Never eat it, cook it, sell it as grain or feed it to animals. Wear gloves when handling it, do not touch your face, and wash your hands with soap after planting. Keep bags locked away from children and livestock, and never reuse empty seed bags for food. Follow the label instructions of the chemical used.
Genetically modified (GM) varieties

Hybrid and conventional breeding move genes only through normal pollination. A **GM** variety has had a specific gene inserted in a laboratory. In Nigeria, GM crops are regulated by the **National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA)**, which must approve a GM variety before it can be released. An insect-resistant cowpea, sold as SAMPEA 20-T, was the first GM food crop approved in Nigeria. GM varieties are sold as certified seed like others, and they may come with stewardship instructions from the seed provider that you must follow.

Keep the receipt, the empty bag and its label until after harvest. If the crop is clearly not the variety you paid for, for example white maize grows from a bag labelled yellow, or many plants are off-type, these items are your evidence when you complain to the dealer, the seed company or NASC.

One plot of a new variety beside one plot of your usual seed is a start, but a single comparison can easily be fooled. A wetter corner, a termite patch or one goat visit can make a poor variety look good. Researchers solve this with **replication** (repeating each variety in several plots) and **randomisation** (letting chance decide where each variety goes). You can do the same on a small scale.
A person filling in a data table
A trial is only as good as the numbers you write down, plot by plot.
A simple trial layout
**Entries:** your usual variety (the check) plus one or two new varieties.
**Blocks:** make three blocks across the field. Each block holds one plot of every variety. Put blocks across any slope or soil change, so each block is as even as possible inside.
**Randomise:** in each block, write the variety names on folded papers and draw them to decide the order.
**Plot size:** for maize, 4 rows of 5 m at 75 cm spacing is practical. The 2 outer rows are borders; you harvest only the 2 middle rows, the **net plot**.
**Same management:** same planting day, spacing, fertiliser, weeding and pest control for every plot.

What to record during the season
**Plant stand:** number of plants in each net plot about 3 weeks after planting and again at harvest.
**Days to 50% silking or flowering:** count days from planting until half the plants show silks. This shows earliness.
**Disease and pest scores:** use a 1 to 5 scale (1 = clean, 5 = severe) for the problem you care about, for example streak virus or leaf blight.
**Lodging:** number of plants fallen or broken before harvest.
**Rain and events:** dry spells, storms, late weeding or animal damage, with dates.

Following the same steps for every plot makes the comparison fair.

Freshly harvested grain still holds water, and wetter grain weighs more. To compare fairly, correct every plot to the same standard moisture. Many maize trials use 15%. Ask an ADP office, a grain buyer or a warehouse to test moisture with a meter, or dry all samples the same way before weighing. The correction formula is: **corrected weight = field weight x (100 minus measured moisture) / (100 minus standard moisture)**.
Worked example: yield of one plot and the trial means
For example, Rukayat in Kaduna harvests her trial. Each net plot is 2 rows x 0.75 m x 5 m = 7.5 m2. The grain from Variety A in Block 1 weighs 4.2 kg at 20% moisture. Standard moisture is 15%.
Scale to a hectare: 3.95 kg / 7.5 m2 x 10,000 m2 = 5,267 kg per hectare, about 5.3 tonnes.
She does the same for all 9 plots. Variety A in blocks 1, 2 and 3: 5,267, 4,800 and 5,100 kg/ha. Mean = 15,167 / 3 = 5,056 kg/ha.
Usual variety in blocks 1, 2 and 3: 4,100, 4,400 and 3,900 kg/ha. Mean = 12,400 / 3 = 4,133 kg/ha.
Difference: 5,056 - 4,133 = 923 kg/ha. Variety A beat the check in every block, not just on average.
Variety A out-yielded her usual seed by about 920 kg per hectare and won in all three blocks, which is far stronger evidence than one side-by-side plot.
Consistency matters as much as the average

If a new variety wins by a lot in one block but loses in the other two, the average can mislead you. Look at each block. If results swing about, repeat the trial for another season or at a second site before deciding.

Choosing the site matters as much as the layout. Avoid old termite mounds, spots where crop residue was burnt, shade from trees and the low corner where water collects. If the field slopes, run each block across the slope so all plots in a block sit at the same height. Plant all plots on the same day with seed from tested lots, and thin to the same number of plants per hole so that plant stand does not decide the winner.

At harvest, count the plants in each net plot before cutting. If one plot lost many plants to termites or animals, note it. A plot with far fewer plants than the others is not a fair test of that variety, and you should mention it in your report rather than quietly using the low yield.

A higher yield is not automatically a better deal. In this module you will turn trial results into a partial budget, keep good seed alive through proper drying and storage, work with research institutes, extension and seed banks, and finish with a written trial report and a 90-day adoption plan.
Partial Budgets: Is the New Variety Worth Its Extra Cost?

Your trial tells you how much more a new variety yields. It does not yet tell you whether it pays. For that, agricultural economists use a **partial budget**. Instead of listing every cost on the farm, you list only what **changes** when you switch: extra income from extra grain, and extra costs such as dearer seed, more fertiliser, and more labour, bags and transport for the bigger harvest. The method is widely taught to extension workers, for example in CIMMYT's manual on turning agronomic data into farmer recommendations.

**Net benefit** = (added income + reduced costs) minus (added costs + reduced income). The **marginal rate of return (MRR)** = net benefit divided by the extra money you had to put in, shown as a percentage. It tells you how many naira you get back for each extra naira spent. Because farming is risky, a small positive return is not enough: CIMMYT's guidance is that farmers usually need a clearly high return, often suggested at 50% to 100% or more, before a change is worth the risk.
Worked example: Rukayat's partial budget for Variety A
For example, Rukayat's trial in the last module showed Variety A, a hybrid, yielding 923 kg per hectare more than her usual saved seed. All prices are illustrative; use the prices in your own market.
Added income: 923 kg x about N600 per kg = N553,800.
Added seed cost: hybrid 20 kg x N5,000 = N100,000, minus her usual saved seed worth N14,000 = N86,000.
Added fertiliser: the hybrid's recommended top-dressing needs about one extra bag, roughly N40,000.
Added harvest costs for the extra grain (labour, shelling, bags, transport): about N15,000. Total added costs: N86,000 + N40,000 + N15,000 = N141,000.

On her trial numbers, every extra N1 spent on Variety A returned about N2.93 on top of getting the N1 back. That is well above the minimum return usually suggested, so the switch looks worthwhile, if the result holds.
Break-even yield and risk tests

Next, ask: how much extra grain do I need just to cover the extra costs? **Break-even yield gain = added costs / grain price.** For Rukayat: N141,000 / N600 = 235 kg per hectare. If the hybrid beats her usual seed by more than about 235 kg, it pays; if less, she loses money.
**Price drops:** at harvest, prices often fall. At N400 per kg, added income is 923 x 400 = N369,200, and net benefit is N369,200 - N141,000 = N228,200. Still positive.
**Bad season:** suppose a dry spell cuts the gain to 200 kg. At N600, added income is N120,000, which is N21,000 less than the added costs. She would lose money that year.
**Cash risk:** the N141,000 is spent at planting, months before harvest. Can she afford to lose it in a bad year without selling food the family needs?

If a hybrid's cash risk is too high, run the same partial budget for an improved OPV. Its yield gain may be smaller, but its seed cost in later seasons is much lower, so its MRR can still be attractive.

Use the price you will actually receive, not the highest price you have heard. If you usually sell soon after harvest, when prices are lowest, use that price. If you will store and sell later, include storage costs such as hermetic bags. Also count your own family labour fairly. Extra days spent harvesting and shelling a bigger crop have a value, even if no cash changes hands.

Finally, remember the seed-saving effect. A hybrid's seed cost repeats every season, while an improved OPV's seed cost falls after the first season if you save seed well. Keeping Good Seed Alive: Saving, Storage and Community Seed Banks
Dry seed properly and check dryness with the salt jar test
Store seed in airtight containers to protect germination and stop weevils
Set up simple rules and records for a community seed bank
Identify research institutes and partners who supply and advise on improved varieties

Selecting good seed is wasted if the seed dies or is eaten by weevils before planting. Seed is alive. It breathes slowly, and heat and moisture make it age fast. The two rules of seed storage are simple: **keep it dry** and **keep it cool**, inside a container that insects and damp air cannot enter.
A young seedling
A well-dried, well-stored seed keeps its power to grow into a strong seedling.
Drying and checking dryness
Dry seed on a clean tarpaulin or raised mat, not on bare soil, turning it several times a day. Cover it at night and when rain threatens.
Avoid very hot surfaces such as zinc roofing or concrete at midday, which can damage the seed embryo.
Do the **salt jar test**: put a handful of seed and two or three spoons of dry table salt in a clean, dry glass jar. Close it tightly, shake for a minute and leave for about 15 minutes.
If salt sticks to the sides of the jar, the seed is still too damp. Dry it for longer and test again. If the salt flows freely, the seed is dry enough to store.
If you can reach a grain moisture meter at an ADP office or warehouse, use it to confirm.
Storing seed
**Hermetic (airtight) bags** such as triple-layer PICS bags, or airtight drums and plastic containers, starve weevils of oxygen and keep damp air out.
Fill containers fully, press out air and seal tightly. Store off the floor, away from walls, in the coolest dry room.
Label each container with crop, variety, season, where it came from and the date stored.
Do a germination test on stored seed two weeks before planting every season.
Do not mix grain chemicals with seed you will eat

If you use a storage insecticide, use only products approved for that use, follow the label dose and waiting time, and keep seed meant for planting clearly separate from food grain. When in doubt, choose hermetic bags, which need no chemicals.
Community seed banks

A **community seed bank** is a store run by a farmer group where members borrow seed at planting and return more after harvest. It keeps good varieties in the community, helps members who lost their seed, and can hold small stocks of improved OPVs bought as certified seed. It works only with clear rules and honest records.

Members borrow seed
Plant and select
Dry and test seed
Return seed with interest
Store and record
Each season the bank's stock should grow if every member returns clean, dry, tested seed.
Worked example: a seed bank ledger

For example, a women's group in Benue State starts a cowpea seed bank with 60 kg of certified seed of an improved variety. The group agrees that each member borrows 4 kg and returns double, 8 kg, of clean, dry, tested seed.
Twelve members borrow 4 kg each: 12 x 4 = 48 kg lent out. Stock left in the bank: 60 - 48 = 12 kg.
After harvest, ten members return 8 kg each: 10 x 8 = 80 kg.
Two members lost their crops to flooding. The group agrees they will return 4 kg each next season, and records this as owed: 8 kg.
New stock: 12 + 80 = 92 kg, with 8 kg owed.
Before storing, a 100-seed germination test is done on each member's returned seed; one lot germinates poorly and is kept for food, not seed.
The bank grows from 60 kg to 92 kg in one season, with records showing who borrowed, who returned, what is owed and which seed passed the quality test.

Your Variety Trial Report and 90-Day Adoption Plan
Write a clear one-to-two-page trial report with methods, results and economics

Your trial becomes truly useful when it is written down so that you, your group and your extension agent can learn from it. A good report is short, honest and full of numbers. It also includes what went wrong, because a storm or late weeding may explain a surprising result.
A person presenting a report
A short, honest report turns one season's work into evidence others can use.
What the report contains
**Goal:** the problem and the trait you were looking for, from your variety profile.
**Varieties and seed:** names, seed class, source, germination test result.
**Methods:** location, planting date, spacing, fertiliser, layout (three blocks, randomised), net plot size.
**Season notes:** rainfall, dry spells, pests, diseases, any damage, with dates.
**Results:** plant stand, days to 50% silking, scores, lodging, and corrected yield per plot and per hectare, with means.
**Economics:** your partial budget, MRR, break-even yield gain and risk tests.
**Decision and reasons:** adopt, re-test or reject, and why.
Simple decision rules

Decide your rules **before** you see the results, so you are not tempted to bend them. For example: adopt if the new variety beats the check in every block, its yield gain is well above the break-even gain, and its MRR passes your minimum. Re-test if it wins on average but not in every block, or if the season was unusual. Reject if it loses on average, fails a must-have trait, or does not pay.
Worked example: applying the rules

For example, Hauwa in Kano tested two varieties against her usual seed. Her rules: adopt if the variety wins in all three blocks and MRR is above 100%; re-test if it wins on average only; reject otherwise.
Variety A: won in all 3 blocks, mean gain 600 kg/ha, break-even gain 250 kg/ha, MRR 140%. All conditions met: adopt.
Variety B: won in 2 of 3 blocks, mean gain 300 kg/ha, MRR 45%. Wins on average but not in every block, and MRR is low: re-test on a small area.
Her usual seed: remains on part of the farm as a safety net while she scales up Variety A.
Scale-up: she plants Variety A on half her maize land next season, not all, because one season is limited evidence.
She keeps the same record sheet so next season's results can be added to this one.
Hauwa's decision is clear and defensible: adopt A on half the land, keep testing B, and keep her usual seed as insurance.
Sharing results honestly

Invite your farmer group to see the plots before harvest, standing at each block so they see the differences themselves. Afterwards, share a short summary on your group's WhatsApp: the varieties, a photo of the plots, the yield table and your partial budget. Say plainly what did not work. A neighbour on sandier soil may get different results, so encourage others to run their own small trial rather than copying your choice.

Spacing the steps across 90 days means seed, cash and land are ready before the rains.
Respect breeders' and companies' rights

Some varieties are protected, and seed companies may not allow their seed to be multiplied and sold by others. Saving seed of a public OPV for your own farm is normal; selling seed to others as a named variety should be done only through proper registration with NASC. Ask your ADP or the seed supplier if you are unsure.

Write the results section mostly as a table: one row per variety, with columns for plant stand, days to 50% silking, disease score, lodging, and the corrected yield in each block plus the mean. Under the table, write two or three plain sentences on what the numbers mean. Readers should be able to see the evidence at a glance and check your arithmetic.

Be honest about the limits. One season at one site cannot prove a variety is better everywhere. If the rains were unusually good or poor, say so. If animals damaged one plot, say which one and how you handled it. A report that admits its weaknesses is more trusted by extension agents and other farmers, and it reminds you to keep testing. It also helps others decide whether your conditions are close enough to theirs for your result to apply.

Finally, store your report safely: keep a paper copy with your farm records and a photo or Google Docs copy on your phone. Next season's report can then sit beside this one, and after two or three seasons you will have your own evidence base for seed decisions.

Every seed in the first generation, called F1, gets one yellow and one white copy. All show yellow grain.
She plants the F1 seed and lets the plants pollinate each other.
In the second generation, three of every four combinations carry yellow.
On a cob of 400 kernels, she expects about 300 yellow and 100 white. That splitting is why saved hybrid seed does not stay true.

In self-pollinated crops like rice, cowpea and groundnut, pollen usually comes from the same flower. Saved seed stays close to its parent.
In maize, the tassel sheds pollen and the wind carries it to the silks of other plants. Pollen from a neighbour's field can change your next crop.

Step by step
Write the cross on the bag, mother first, and leave it to harvest.
Bag the ear shoot before silks show
Cut back the silks, re-bag at once
Same afternoon, bag the father tassel
Next morning, collect the pollen
Pour on the silks, cover the ear
Label the bag and tag
Step 1. Cover the ear shoot with a shoot bag as soon as it appears, before any silk comes out.
Step 2. When silks emerge, cut them straight across in the afternoon, and re-bag at once.
Step 3. The same afternoon, cover the father's tassel with a tassel bag and staple it.
Step 4. Next morning, after the dew dries, bend the tassel and tap the bag so pollen falls inside.
Step 5. Lift the shoot bag quickly, pour the pollen over the silks, and cover the ear with the tassel bag.
Step 6. Write the cross on the bag and a tag, mother first, with the date.
For tomato, remove the anthers from a bud before it opens. That is called emasculation.

Three blocks across the field

A single comparison can be fooled by a wet corner. Step 1. Choose your usual variety, the check, plus one or two new ones.
Step 2. Make three blocks across any slope. Each block holds every variety once.
Step 3. In each block, draw folded papers to decide the order.
Step 4. Plant 4 rows of 5 m. The outer rows are borders. Harvest only the 2 middle rows, the net plot.

Rukayat's added costs for Variety A
For example, Rukayat's Variety A, a hybrid, out-yielded her usual seed by 923 kg per hectare.

Extra seed cost
Extra fertiliser

A partial budget lists only what changes when you switch. For example, Rukayat's hybrid gave 923 kg per hectare more than her usual seed. At about 600 naira per kg, that is 553,800 naira of added income.
Now the added costs. Hybrid seed costs 100,000 naira, minus her usual saved seed worth 14,000, so 86,000 naira extra.
The hybrid needs about one extra bag of fertiliser, roughly 40,000 naira.
Harvesting, shelling, bags and transport for the extra grain add about 15,000 naira.
Her total added costs are 141,000 naira.
Does it pay?
Net benefit, return and break-even
Always test against a lower price and a bad season.
Net benefit: income minus added costs
Return: net benefit / added costs
Break-even: added costs / grain price
Test a lower grain price
Test a bad season
Net benefit is the added income minus the added costs. For Rukayat, 553,800 minus 141,000 is 412,800 naira.
The marginal rate of return is net benefit divided by the extra money spent. Here it is about 293%. Farming is risky, so aim for 50% to 100% or more.
Break-even is added costs divided by the grain price. 141,000 divided by 600 is 235 kg. Below that gain, she loses money.
If the price drops to 400 naira at harvest, her net benefit is still 228,200 naira.
But if a dry spell cuts the gain to 200 kg, she loses money that year.
Use the price you will actually receive, not the highest price you have heard.
Keep seed alive
Dry it, test it, seal it
Keep seed dry, keep it cool, keep air and insects out.
Dry on a tarpaulin, not bare soil
Avoid hot zinc or concrete at midday
Salt jar test: seed plus dry salt
Salt sticks? Dry longer
Seal in airtight bags, off the floor
Seed is alive, and heat and moisture make it age fast. Dry it on a clean tarpaulin or raised mat.
Avoid very hot zinc roofing or concrete at midday, which can damage the seed.
Then do the salt jar test. Put a handful of seed and two or three spoons of dry salt in a dry glass jar. Shake it and wait about 15 minutes.
If salt sticks to the jar, the seed is still too damp. Dry it longer and test again.
Store it in airtight bags such as PICS bags, which starve weevils of oxygen. Label each one.
If you use a storage insecticide, use only an approved product at the label dose, and keep planting seed apart from food grain.

10 members return 8 kg each: 80 kg
2 flooded members owe 8 kg

In a community seed bank, members borrow seed at planting and return more after harvest. For example, a women's group in Benue State starts with 60 kg of certified cowpea seed.
Twelve members borrow 4 kg each.
After harvest, ten members return double, 8 kg each. That is 80 kg.
Two members lost their crops to flooding. The group records 8 kg as owed next season.
The stock grows to 92 kg. Every returned lot gets a germination test, and one poor lot is kept for food, not seed.
